reasons: technical: The post says OBI assigns its own trace IDs and that the load client's traceparent does not shape them. Yet the sample trace's orders server span has a parent (e76355175e7d3f75) that is not among the trace's spans, and load appears on the map as an instrumented service. The post never shows the evidence for its trace-ID claim and leaves the dangling parent unexplained, so a reader cannot tell whether the incoming header partly shaped the context. Fix: Quote the lab's count of traces carrying the caller's trace ID (the 'traced under the ID the caller sent' line, or the matching EKS check). Then say in one sentence what the parent span ID is, for example load's client span exported in another trace, or a parent span ID taken from the incoming header. If the run cannot settle it, say the span ID is an open question and soften 'doesn't shape them' to what was measured.
outside claim without a known source: OBI loads its own Java agent by default for TLS tracing, virtual-thread correlation and runtime metrics, and javaagent.enabled turns it off
outside claim without a known source: OBI covers every namespace by default and service discovery settings can narrow that
outside claim without a known source: Splunk describes an inferred service as one it deduces from a caller's span

Every headline number matches a corroborated contract line: 2 of 2 services sent their own spans, 0 restarts on 3 pods with UIDs kept, joined traces went from 0 of 30 to 30 of 30, the agent library was mapped in both JVMs, and p95 rose 2.58 ms against 7.58 ms of noise.

The before-checks could have failed. The lab stops if cluster data never reaches Splunk or if the map already holds the services, and it compares pod UIDs, so a replaced pod cannot pass as 0 restarts.

Claims stay within the evidence. The inferred=true flag is reported as a fact with no cause given, and the post says a library mapping shows only that the library is present. The latency result is limited to one cluster at one rate.

One loose end: the post says OBI assigns its own trace IDs, but the sample trace's orders server span has a parent that is not in the trace. A sharp reader will ask where that parent came from, and the post does not show the lab line behind the trace-ID claim.

The reader and the decision are clear: a platform engineer wants a first map before asking any team to change a deployment. The title delivers exactly what the first value showed, and the second value is presented honestly as a separate step.

It has findings beyond the docs. The map draws orders -> inventory while 0 of 30 traces join until propagation is on. The pods keep their identity, verified by UID. OBI loads a Java agent into running JVMs, and the post gives a result on Amazon Linux 2023.
The trade-offs on privileges, the injected agent, namespace scope and latency sit in the body as things to plan for, which is the right tone.
Some lines read as generated, such as 'Here's one with both values on:', a TL;DR that repeats the body, and evenly sized sections. The 'Use it for your own services' bullets mostly restate the docs.

Demand evidence is weak. The only signal is one OBI issue with a few comments, and it is about Java agent injection into non-root JVMs, not about getting a first service map. There is no search volume and no linked reaction to this topic.
Splunk fits naturally because the chart value and the APM map are the subject, and the title credits the product with the result.

The headline uses plain words for the situation (one Helm value, running Java services, EKS), but nothing shows these are the words readers search with. Without a real demand signal this cannot score above 3.

claims.text: OBI is a beta feature in Splunk Observability Cloud and runs as a DaemonSet capturing traces and request metrics from outside the process
OBI loads its own Java agent by default for TLS tracing, virtual-thread correlation and runtime metrics, and javaagent.enabled turns it off
OBI covers every namespace by default and service discovery settings can narrow that
Splunk describes an inferred service as one it deduces from a caller's span
OBI's outgoing propagation is off by default
Proxies and load balancers can affect propagation
Async frameworks need their own check for context propagation
The chart's default runs OBI privileged with host PID and host network, and the guide lists a reduced capability set
The chart guide names Ubuntu as its tested node OS
Reduced capabilities can affect Java agent injection into non-root JVMs
Splunk recommends combining OBI with language agents
Language agents join the JVM at startup, so the pods have to roll
The usual route to a service map means instrumenting each service, planning a rollout and waiting for it
OBI assigns its own trace IDs, so the load client's traceparent header does not shape them
It takes about 25 minutes from an empty account

brief.reader: Platform engineer running Java services on EKS who wants a first service map before asking any team to change a deployment
brief.decision: Whether to turn on OBI through the Splunk OTel Collector chart as a first layer across a cluster, before rolling out language agents
brief.question: Can I get services that are already running on EKS onto the Splunk APM map without restarting a pod, and what do I get from it?
brief.takeaway: You can decide from measured numbers: what one Helm value puts on the map for running services, what it does to the pods, and whether traces across nodes need a second value.
brief.adds: Existing pages state that OBI needs no restart and list what it captures. This post measures it on EKS on Amazon Linux 2023: services on the map, each pod's UID and restart count before and after, whether one trace spans two nodes with and without propagation, the Java helper OBI loads, and the p95 latency added.
brief.open_question: With obi.enabled=true alone on chart 0.163.1, how many running services reach the Splunk APM map, how many pod restarts does it add, and how many services share one trace across two nodes with and without outgoing header propagation?
tradeoffs: OBI first for a broad map, or a language agent for deeper framework detail
A privileged DaemonSet with host PID and host network, or the chart's documented reduced capabilities
Every namespace by default, or a namespace filter
Outgoing header propagation on, or kept at its default
